cues.text: Chapter six is about caching and materialised views.
Both ideas share one goal: avoid doing expensive work again and again, by keeping a ready-made answer close at hand.
But as you will see, a stored answer can go out of date, and that is the central trade-off of this whole chapter.
Let us begin with caching.
There are three kinds to distinguish.
First, a buffer cache stores database pages.
That is the database engine keeping recently used pages of data in memory, so it does not have to fetch them again.
Second, an application cache, also called a query-result cache, stores derived results.
Here the thing kept is not a raw page, but the answer to some computation or query.
Third, a distributed cache, for example Redis, serves multiple application instances.
So if you run several copies of an application, they can all share one cache.
Next, how do we read from and write to a cache?
The source describes several patterns.
In cache-aside, the application reads the cache first.
If the value is not there, which we call a miss, it reads the database and then populates the cache with the result.
In write-through, the cache is updated along with the authoritative write, according to the design.
The authoritative write means the write to the real database, the source of truth.
In write-back, persistence is deferred.
The data is saved to durable storage later, which means there is a risk of loss if the cached data is not durable.
Now, cached values go stale, so we need ways to control that.
A TTL, or time to live, limits staleness: each entry expires after a set time.
Invalidation removes outdated entries when the underlying data changes.
And when the cache is full, eviction policies decide what to throw out.
Two examples are LRU, least recently used, and LFU, least frequently used.
There is also a well-known danger called cache stampede.
This occurs when many callers all try to regenerate an expired value at the same moment.
Imagine a popular entry expires, and hundreds of requests all hit the database at once to rebuild it.
Two things can help: request coalescing, where concurrent requests for the same value are combined so only one does the work, and staggered expiry, where entries do not all expire at the same time.
One more rule, and it is a serious one: never rely on a shared cache key that omits tenant or security scope.
If the key does not say whose data it is, one tenant, or one user, could be served another's cached result.
Now to views.
A normal view stores a query definition, and it is generally evaluated when it is accessed.
A materialised view is different.
It stores its result, and therefore it must be refreshed.
There are several ways to do that.
A full refresh recomputes the whole result.
Incremental maintenance applies only the changes, where that is supported.
A scheduled refresh trades freshness against cost: refresh more often and the data is fresher but costs more.
And on-demand or event-driven refresh fits other requirements, where you refresh when asked, or when something happens.
Here is a PostgreSQL example.
Let us go through it line by line.
The first statement creates a materialized view named daily_visits.
Its query selects clinic_id, and also visited_at converted to a date, which is given the name day, and a count of all rows, named n.
It reads from the visit table, and groups by clinic_id and that same date conversion.
So the result is the number of visits per clinic per day, and, because it is materialised, that result is stored.
The second statement creates a unique index, named daily_visits_key, on the view, covering clinic_id and day together.
Each clinic and day pair appears only once, because of the grouping, and the unique index is what makes the next step possible.
The third statement refreshes the materialized view, using the CONCURRENTLY option, which refreshes it without the usual blocking of readers.
The source adds some conditions.
This PostgreSQL example requires a populated view and a suitable unique index for concurrent refresh.
And finally, views are not automatic security boundaries.
Privileges and the underlying access paths matter, so you cannot assume that a view on its own protects the data beneath it.
